explanations.explanation: That's the offer, friend. Hezekiah says, "I have done wrong; withdraw from me, and I will pay whatever you demand from me" (2 Kings 18:14). He doesn't even ask what the number is first. That's handing someone your wallet and saying "take what you need," and I think it shows how much weight he was carrying.

explanations.answer: To hand over his own throne
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Hezekiah offers to pay, not to move out of the palace. His words are "I will pay whatever you demand from me" (2 Kings 18:14). A few verses later the text still calls him "King Hezekiah" (2 Kings 18:17), so the seat stays his.

explanations.answer: To send troops for his wars
explanations.explanation: Soldiers never come up in his message, friend. What he puts on the table is payment: "I will pay whatever you demand from me" (2 Kings 18:14). Then the king of Assyria answers with silver and gold, not an army from Judah. The offer is money from start to finish.

explanations.answer: The LORD's house and the palace treasuries
explanations.explanation: Right where the text puts it, friend. Hezekiah gave "all the silver that was found in the house of the LORD and in the treasuries of the royal palace" (2 Kings 18:15). Two places, and he emptied the silver out of both. That's turning out every pocket and then checking the couch cushions too.

explanations.answer: The cities of the Philistines he defeated
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't send him to the Philistines, friend. It says the silver came from "the house of the LORD and in the treasuries of the royal palace" (2 Kings 18:15). That's his own temple and his own palace. Nobody else's cities get mentioned in this verse.

explanations.answer: The ships that came in from Tarshish
explanations.explanation: No ships pull into this story, friend. The verse says Hezekiah gave "all the silver that was found in the house of the LORD and in the treasuries of the royal palace" (2 Kings 18:15). The money is already inside Jerusalem. He just has to go gather it up.

Gold it is. The text says Hezekiah "stripped the gold with which he had plated the doors and doorposts of the temple of the LORD, and he gave it to the king of Assyria" (2 Kings 18:16). He had put that gold on there himself, and now he takes it back off. I think that was a long walk down the temple hallway.

Close in sound, but not what the text says. The plating Hezekiah took off was gold, not bronze (2 Kings 18:16). He had plated the doors and doorposts with it himself. Then he stripped it and handed it over to the king of Assyria.

The text doesn't mention cedar, friend. What came off the doors and doorposts was gold: "he stripped the gold with which he had plated" them (2 Kings 18:16). Plating is a covering, and that covering is what he gave away. So gold is the word that fits the blank.

I know it feels like he should leave after getting paid. But the text says the opposite: "Nevertheless, the king of Assyria sent the Tartan, the Rabsaris, and the Rabshakeh, along with a great army, from Lachish to King Hezekiah at Jerusalem" (2 Kings 18:17). That word "Nevertheless" carries the whole verse. The payment didn't send him home.

Yes, friend. Hezekiah paid, and the verse still opens with "Nevertheless" (2 Kings 18:17). The king of Assyria sent the Tartan, the Rabsaris and the Rabshakeh with a great army, and they advanced up to Jerusalem. The silver and gold didn't make anybody turn around.

Not this time, friend. The Assyrians "called for the king," but the king doesn't walk out (2 Kings 18:18). Three of his men go instead: Eliakim, Shebnah and Joah. Hezekiah stays inside and sends his team.

That's it. The Assyrians called for the king, and out came Eliakim the palace administrator, Shebnah the scribe and Joah the recorder (2 Kings 18:18). Hezekiah himself stays behind. They show up to a meeting that asked for the boss, and the boss sends his people.

Right. The Rabshakeh asks, "What is the basis of this confidence of yours?" (2 Kings 18:19). Basis is just the ground it stands on. He wants to know what Hezekiah is leaning on, and he's about to start poking at every answer.

He isn't asking about how long, friend. His question is "What is the basis of this confidence of yours?" (2 Kings 18:19). He wants to know what the confidence stands on. Nothing in the question is about its timing.

explanations.answer: Who it is meant to impress
explanations.explanation: Good guess for a man with a big audience, but that isn't what he asks. The question is "What is the basis of this confidence of yours?" (2 Kings 18:19). He's asking what Hezekiah's confidence rests on. Nobody's being impressed in that sentence.

Egypt is the name he picks. He says, "Look now, you are trusting in Egypt" (2 Kings 18:21). He's the one making the guess, and he says it with total confidence. He sounds like a man who has already read your mail.
Babylon never comes up in his speech, friend. The Rabshakeh says, "Look now, you are trusting in Egypt" (2 Kings 18:21). That's the one place he points to. The blank wants Egypt.
Moab isn't in this speech, friend. What he says is, "Look now, you are trusting in Egypt" (2 Kings 18:21). He names Pharaoh king of Egypt right in the same verse. So Egypt fills the blank.

He does bring it up. The Rabshakeh asks, "is He not the One whose high places and altars Hezekiah has removed, saying to Judah and Jerusalem: 'You must worship before this altar in Jerusalem'?" (2 Kings 18:22). He raises it as a point against Hezekiah. I'm just telling you what he says, friend.

The text says he does. The Rabshakeh asks, "is He not the One whose high places and altars Hezekiah has removed…" (2 Kings 18:22). He then repeats the words about worshiping before the altar in Jerusalem. It's right there in his speech.

explanations.answer: Judah has to find riders for them
explanations.explanation: There's the catch. He says, "I will give you two thousand horses…" and then adds that it's only if Judah can put riders on them (2 Kings 18:23). That's offering free horses to someone with nobody to sit on them. It's a gift that sounds generous and is really a dare.

explanations.answer: Judah has to pay for every horse
explanations.explanation: Money isn't the catch here, friend. He says, "I will give you two thousand horses," and the condition that follows is about riders (2 Kings 18:23). The horses are offered as a gift. What he's questioning is whether Judah has anyone to ride them.

explanations.answer: Judah has to return them by spring
explanations.explanation: Nobody mentions a deadline, friend. The Rabshakeh offers "two thousand horses," then says it's only if Judah can put riders on them (2 Kings 18:23). The condition is about riders, not a return date. There's no spring in this verse.

Yes, the LORD is the name he uses. The Rabshakeh says, "The LORD Himself said to me, 'Go up against this land and destroy it.'" (2 Kings 18:25). Those are his words in his speech, and the text just records them. He's using the very name Hezekiah trusts.

Baal isn't the name he uses, friend. The Rabshakeh says, "The LORD Himself said to me, 'Go up against this land and destroy it.'" (2 Kings 18:25). He chooses the name of the God Judah trusts. That's what makes the claim so bold.

Dagon doesn't come up in his speech, friend. The Rabshakeh says, "The LORD Himself said to me, 'Go up against this land and destroy it.'" (2 Kings 18:25). He names the LORD, the same God Hezekiah trusts. So the blank wants LORD.

That's their request. Eliakim, Shebnah and Joah say, "Please speak to your servants in Aramaic, since we understand it. Do not speak with us in Hebrew in the hearing of the people on the wall" (2 Kings 18:26). They say "please," and they say it politely. I think they were hoping to keep this talk away from the wall.

They don't ask for a private meeting with the king, friend. Their request is about language: "Please speak to your servants in Aramaic, since we understand it" (2 Kings 18:26). They also ask him not to use Hebrew where the people on the wall can hear. So the ask is Aramaic.

No one asks him to reschedule, friend. They ask, "Please speak to your servants in Aramaic, since we understand it" (2 Kings 18:26). The request is about which language he speaks, and they want it now. A different day isn't in there.

He says no. The Rabshakeh answers, "Has my master sent me to speak these words only to you and your master, and not to the men sitting on the wall…" (2 Kings 18:27). He's saying the people on the wall are meant to hear it too. I think this part of the passage is a heavy one.

That's right. The Rabshakeh asks whether his master sent him "to speak these words only to you and your master, and not to the men sitting on the wall" (2 Kings 18:27). He won't keep it private, and he then speaks of what lies ahead for those men. I think this one is a hard thing to hear.

He does, and he's not shy about it. "Then the Rabshakeh stood and called out loudly in Hebrew" (2 Kings 18:28). Hebrew is the very language the three officials asked him not to use in front of the wall. He heard their request and did the exact opposite.

explanations.answer: Walks back to the army camp
explanations.explanation: He doesn't go anywhere, friend. The text says he "stood and called out loudly in Hebrew" (2 Kings 18:28). He's staying right where he is and getting louder. Nobody is heading back to camp.
No letter in this scene, friend. The Rabshakeh "stood and called out loudly in Hebrew" (2 Kings 18:28). He's speaking out loud to the people on the wall. The message goes out by voice, not paper.

It's the other way around, friend. He tells the people, "Do not let Hezekiah deceive you; he cannot deliver you from my hand" (2 Kings 18:29). He's saying Hezekiah can't do it. The whole speech is built to make the people doubt their king.

Right. The Rabshakeh says, "Do not let Hezekiah deceive you; he cannot deliver you from my hand" (2 Kings 18:29). He's telling the wall that Hezekiah has nothing to offer them. He's trying to make them look somewhere else.

He does. The Rabshakeh says, "Do not let Hezekiah persuade you to trust in the LORD when he says, 'The LORD will surely deliver us; this city will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria'" (2 Kings 18:30). He quotes the promise so he can tell the people not to believe it. He's repeating Hezekiah's own words back to the crowd.

The text says he does. The Rabshakeh says, "Do not let Hezekiah persuade you to trust in the LORD when he says, 'The LORD will surely deliver us…'" (2 Kings 18:30). He quotes the promise out loud. Then he tells the people not to believe it.

explanations.answer: He will take them to a land like their own
explanations.explanation: That's his promise. The king of Assyria will come "and take you away to a land like your own," a land of grain, new wine, bread, vineyards, olive trees and honey (2 Kings 18:32). It sounds like a nice offer. But notice it still says "take you away."

explanations.answer: He will let them stay in Jerusalem for good
explanations.explanation: That's not what he says, friend. He says he will "come and take you away to a land like your own" (2 Kings 18:32). Taking away is the opposite of staying. The pitch is a move, not a permanent home in Jerusalem.

explanations.answer: He will keep Hezekiah in charge of them
explanations.explanation: He says the opposite, friend. In the same breath he tells the people, "do not listen to Hezekiah" (2 Kings 18:32). What he promises is to "take you away to a land like your own." Hezekiah isn't in that picture.

Samaria is the one he names. He asks, "Where are the gods of Hamath and Arpad? Where are the gods of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah? Have they delivered Samaria from my hand?" (2 Kings 18:34). It's the last name in his list. He's piling up places to make a point.

Damascus isn't in his list, friend. The Rabshakeh names Hamath, Arpad, Sepharvaim, Hena and Ivvah, then asks, "Have they delivered Samaria from my hand?" (2 Kings 18:34). Samaria is the place he saves for last. That's the word for the blank.

Tyre doesn't make his list, friend. He asks about Hamath, Arpad, Sepharvaim, Hena and Ivvah, and then, "Have they delivered Samaria from my hand?" (2 Kings 18:34). The place he names is Samaria. So that's the one that fits.

He does. After running through the lands, the Rabshakeh asks, "How then can the LORD deliver Jerusalem from my hand?" (2 Kings 18:35). That's where his whole list was headed. He's saying that if no other god stopped him, neither will the God Judah trusts.

The text says he does ask it. The Rabshakeh finishes by saying, "How then can the LORD deliver Jerusalem from my hand?" (2 Kings 18:35). Everything before it, the list of lands and gods, was leading up to that question. It's the last line of his speech.

Silent as a cookie jar at midnight. "The people remained silent and did not answer a word" (2 Kings 18:36). After all that loud talking, nobody on the wall says anything. That takes some self-control.

explanations.answer: They shout right back at him
explanations.explanation: Nobody shouts, friend. The text says "the people remained silent and did not answer a word" (2 Kings 18:36). He did all the yelling and they gave him nothing back. Quiet was the whole answer.

The gates stay put, friend. What the text says is that "the people remained silent and did not answer a word" (2 Kings 18:36). Nobody opens anything, and nobody says anything. They just stay quiet on the wall.

That's the reason the text gives. The people stayed silent "for Hezekiah had commanded, 'Do not answer him'" (2 Kings 18:36). A whole wall of people heard that speech and still held their tongues. Now that's following instructions.

The text gives a reason, and it's the command. The people remained silent "for Hezekiah had commanded, 'Do not answer him'" (2 Kings 18:36). So the silence wasn't random. The king had told them to say nothing, and they did.

That's the sight. Eliakim, Shebna and Joah "came to Hezekiah with their clothes torn, and they relayed to him the words of the Rabshakeh" (2 Kings 18:37). They went out in clothes and came back in rags. I think that tells you how heavy that morning was.
Not covered, friend. The text says they came to Hezekiah "with their clothes torn" (2 Kings 18:37). That's the detail about how they looked. Nothing is said about their heads.

Nothing about their feet, friend. The text says they came to Hezekiah "with their clothes torn" (2 Kings 18:37). Then they told him what the Rabshakeh had said. The torn clothes are the detail the verse gives.
